title: Self-Portrait in a Fur-Trimmed Robe
medium: Paint on limewood; binder not specified in reviewed record
credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München. Albrecht Dürer, Selbstbildnis im Pelzrock, 1500. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/Qlx2QpQ4Xq CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
description: Dürer faces the viewer almost symmetrically, with long hair framing his face and one hand touching the fur of his robe. Against the dark ground, the face, fingers and individual strands of hair become unusually distinct. The inscriptions share the space on either side of his head.
importance: The frontal arrangement gives a self-portrait the gravity more often associated with a sacred image. Its importance lies partly in that claim for the status of the artist. Look closely at the fur and hair as well: the intellectual ambition is inseparable from the demonstration of painterly control.

title: Saints Cosmas and Damian Saved
catalogueTitle: Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian Salvaged
credit: Fra Angelico. Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian Salvaged. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/fra-angelico/saint-cosmas-and-saint-damian-salvaged-1440
description: Fra Angelico distributes the story across a brightly coloured landscape and architectural setting. Groups of figures appear at different points, connected by paths, changes of level and repeated gestures. The small scale rewards a slow search for the sequence of actions.
importance: This narrative panel demonstrates how a single painted field can contain more than one moment. Its clarity depends on careful organisation rather than on a single dominant figure. It provides a useful contrast to the concentrated encounter in Antonello's Virgin of the Annunciation.

title: Virgin of the Annunciation
credit: Antonello da Messina. Virgin of the Annunciation. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
description: A woman in a dark blue mantle looks up from an open book, her hands crossed before her chest. Antonello places her close to the picture's edge, with little surrounding detail. The light on her face and fingers makes the small changes of pose unusually legible.
importance: The religious encounter is concentrated into a human response. Instead of supplying a large setting, the painting makes the viewer attend to face, gesture and the interruption of reading. Its economy provides a strong counterpoint to the multi-episode narrative in Fra Angelico's panel.

title: Madonna of the Curtain
credit: Madonna della Tenda. WikiArt; Raphael. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
description: Raphael gathers the Virgin and children into a close arrangement of faces, hands and turning bodies. A dark curtain helps frame the group, while the child's upward gaze draws the viewer back towards the Virgin. The figures overlap without losing the clarity of their individual poses.
importance: The painting shows how affection can be made visible through composition. Its significance here is the balance between natural-looking contact and a carefully organised group. Compare the meeting of hands and eyes with the more frontal, isolated figure in Antonello's panel.

title: Self-Portrait as a Young Man
medium: Paint on oak; binder not specified in reviewed record
credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Alte Pinakothek München. Rembrandt (Harmensz. van Rijn), Jugendliches Selbstbildnis, 1629. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/y7GE1PmGPV CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
description: Rembrandt turns his head towards the light, leaving much of the face in shadow beneath unruly hair. The white collar and a few lit curls stand out against a restrained background. The uneven visibility makes looking itself part of the encounter.
importance: The painting uses the artist's own face to investigate light, surface and expression. Its importance becomes clearer beside Dürer's formal self-portrait: the two works construct artistic identity through very different poses and degrees of clarity, without either being merely an unmediated likeness.

title: Sunflowers
credit: © Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen – Neue Pinakothek München. Vincent van Gogh, Sonnenblumen, 1888. https://www.sammlung.pinakothek.de/de/artwork/Y0GR9B7LRX CC BY-SA 4.0; compressed study reproduction.
description: A bunch of sunflowers fills a vase against a blue-green background. Van Gogh distinguishes open blooms, seed heads and curling petals through changes of shape and paint. The yellow tabletop and vessel connect the flowers to the lower part of the canvas.
importance: This is one particular painting in the sunflower sequence, and its colours and arrangement matter. The image shows how a still life can sustain variation within a narrow family of hues. Follow individual flower heads to see how repetition creates differences rather than a uniform pattern.

title: Monet in His Studio Boat
credit: Édouard Manet. Monet in his Studio Boat. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/edouard-manet/monet-in-his-floating-studio-1874
description: Manet shows Monet working inside a small covered boat, with another figure nearby. Dark structural lines frame pale clothing and patches of water, while the surrounding river remains loosely painted. The craft is both a subject in the scene and a place for making pictures.
importance: The work connects the practice of painting outdoors with an image of a fellow artist at work. It is especially useful beside the landscapes in this guide: the conditions of observation become visible. The brisk handling also gives the picture a character distinct from a formal studio portrait.

title: The Road to Hampton Court
credit: Alfred Sisley. The Road to Hampton Court. Image credit: Alfred Sisley. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). Resized and JPEG-compressed; selected source frame preserved.
description: A broad path follows the water towards a small structure in the distance. Sisley balances the warm ground with the cooler river and sky, using small figures to establish scale. Repeated trees and banks draw the eye through the otherwise open view.
importance: The painting demonstrates how a simple route can organise a landscape. Its value beside Pissarro's Upper Norwood lies in the comparison: both depend on recession along a road, yet the placement of water, buildings and sky changes the experience of space.
